moments.title: Weeghman Park opens
moments.text: Restaurant owner Charles Weeghman's new ballpark at Clark and Addison opened for the Chicago Whales of the Federal League, who beat Kansas City in the first game.

moments.title: The Cubs move in
moments.text: After the Federal League folded, Weeghman bought the Cubs and moved them to his park. They won their first game there 7 to 6 over Cincinnati in 11 innings.

moments.title: Renamed Wrigley Field
moments.text: Under owner William Wrigley Jr., the park, called Cubs Park for several years, took the Wrigley name. Some sources date the change to 1927.

moments.title: Ivy on the outfield walls
moments.text: Ivy was planted on the brick outfield walls in 1937, giving the park its best-known look.

moments.title: The lights go on
moments.text: The Cubs played their first night game at home, the last major league team to do so. Rain stopped it after three and a half innings, so the first official night game came the next day.

moments.title: A National Historic Landmark
moments.text: The National Park Service named Wrigley Field a National Historic Landmark.

moments.title: Today: the Friendly Confines
moments.text: The Cubs still play at Clark and Addison in the second-oldest ballpark in the major leagues, after Boston's Fenway Park.

facts.label: First night game
facts.note: Rained out; first official night game Aug 9, 1988.

checked.notes: Opening Apr 23, 1914 for the Federal League Whales and the Cubs' first game Apr 20, 1916 confirmed (Wikipedia, NPS, SABR). Renaming: 1926 per Wikipedia and Britannica, 1927 per SABR; the story keeps 1926. First night game Aug 8, 1988 (rained out), first official Aug 9 (MLB, History.com). Ivy: often credited to Bill Veeck in 1937, but MLB.com notes a photo shows ivy earlier that season and credits the planting differently, so no planter is named. NHL 2020 and 'second-oldest' (NPS) confirmed.
